message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This year's survey gives the Executive Team a clear and positive story, and I think it is a robust one. We used the same validated six-question index as last year, administered by an independent provider under strict confidentiality, so the year-on-year comparison is genuinely like for like. We went out of our way to reach colleagues without computer access, with paper copies and protected time. More than 1,100 colleagues responded, comfortably above the provider's robustness benchmark. The results are encouraging at every level: the overall index is the highest since 2019, every division improved, and the biggest gain came in Repairs and Maintenance, exactly where we concentrated our 2025 investment. The theme data reinforce this, with the largest single improvement on tools and equipment. We have also been honest about the weak spot, workload, and tied it to a specific, measurable cause in Housing Management vacancies. I believe the conclusion that the engagement programme worked, and should be extended, is well supported.
</author>

<document>
2026 Employee Engagement Survey: Results Report
People Analytics Team, Brightwell Housing Association, April 2026

1. Summary
The 2026 engagement survey ran from 2 to 20 March and 1,150 colleagues responded. The overall engagement index rose from 65 to 68, its highest level since the survey began in 2019. This report sets out results by division and theme and recommends priorities for 2026-27.

2. Method
All 1,980 employees on the payroll on 1 March were invited by email, with paper questionnaires and protected time offered to repairs operatives without regular computer access. The survey was administered by an external provider and was confidential: no results are reported for groups of fewer than ten respondents. The engagement index is the mean of six questions on pride, advocacy, intention to stay, motivation, discretionary effort and satisfaction, scaled to 0-100. The questions are unchanged from 2025, so year-on-year comparisons are like for like.

3. Response and engagement by division
Table 1. Response rates and engagement index by division
Division | Headcount 2026 | Responses 2026 | Response rate 2026 | Response rate 2025 | Engagement 2025 | Engagement 2026
Repairs and Maintenance | 820 | 254 | 31% | 64% | 58 | 63
Housing Management | 610 | 427 | 70% | 78% | 69 | 70
Customer Services | 340 | 228 | 67% | 74% | 66 | 68
Central Services | 210 | 141 | 67% | 81% | 72 | 71
Total | 1,980 | 1,050 | 53% | 72% | 65 | 68

The overall response rate fell from 72% to 53%, which remains above the 50% benchmark our provider regards as robust for organisations of our size.

Every division improved its engagement score this year. The largest gain was in Repairs and Maintenance, up five points to 63. Repairs has historically been our least engaged division, and in 2025 it was the focus of a major programme: new vans and tablets for all operatives, a revised bonus scheme and monthly team briefings led by the Director of Property. The results suggest this investment is paying off.

4. Results by theme
Table 2. Theme scores (percentage agreeing), organisation-wide
Theme | 2025 | 2026 | Change
My manager supports my development | 61% | 66% | +5
I have the tools to do my job well | 54% | 62% | +8
I understand the organisation's priorities | 70% | 72% | +2
Workload is manageable | 49% | 47% | -2
I would recommend Brightwell as a place to work | 58% | 63% | +5

Tools and equipment showed the biggest improvement of any theme, consistent with the investment in Repairs. Workload remains the weakest area and is the only theme to decline. Free-text comments on workload most often referred to vacancy cover in Housing Management, where 41 posts were vacant at the time of the survey.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Extend the Repairs model of regular director-led briefings to Housing Management and Customer Services in 2026-27, given the improvement it has delivered in Repairs.
5.2 Prioritise recruitment to Housing Management vacancies, with a target to halve the vacancy count by October.
5.3 Repeat the survey in March 2027 with the same questions and method.

6. Conclusion
2026 shows real and broad-based progress. Engagement is at its highest level since 2019, every division improved, and the division where we invested most improved most. The Executive Team can be confident that the 2025 engagement programme worked, and should extend its most effective elements across the organisation.
</document>
response:
# Review: 2026 Employee Engagement Survey Results Report

The report is clearly written. The method section is good, and recommending a repeat with the same questions is sensible. However, the data in the report's own tables do not support several of its headline claims. In two cases the text contradicts the tables, and the central conclusion, that the Repairs investment worked, is exposed to a problem the report doesn't discuss. I'd fix these before the report goes to the Executive Team, because an attentive reader will find them.

## Factual errors

**1. The respondent count is wrong.** The Summary says 1,150 responded, and your description says "more than 1,100". Table 1 shows 1,050, and the division figures (254 + 427 + 228 + 141) also sum to 1,050. The 53% response rate is calculated on 1,050, so 1,150 is the error.

**2. "Every division improved" is false.** Central Services fell from 72 to 71. This claim appears three times (Section 3, Section 6 and your summary). A one-point fall is probably noise, but the report should say "three of four divisions improved; Central Services was broadly stable".

## The main problem: the Repairs response rate halved

This is the most important issue, and the report passes over it in one sentence.

- Repairs response fell from **64% to 31%**, a drop of 33 points. Other divisions fell 7 to 14 points.
- 31% is well below the provider's 50% robustness benchmark. The overall 53% clears it only because the other divisions offset Repairs. The benchmark is being applied at organisation level to justify a **division-level** conclusion it doesn't support.
- When response collapses like this, the remaining respondents are rarely typical. Engaged staff are more likely to complete surveys. The five-point Repairs gain could therefore be partly or wholly a change in **who answered**, not in how people feel. With the data presented, we cannot tell these apart.
- This affects the report's main causal story. The division with the biggest claimed improvement is also the division with by far the least reliable sample.
- The collapse is itself a finding worth investigating. Paper copies and protected time were offered, yet response halved. Possible causes include the paper process not being delivered as planned, survey fatigue, or distrust, perhaps linked to the revised bonus scheme. Any of these would matter to the Executive Team.

**Suggested fixes:**
- Report the Repairs figure with an explicit caveat.
- Ask the provider whether Repairs respondents differ from non-respondents on available characteristics such as team, tenure, grade or paper vs online.
- Check whether the paper route actually reached operatives.
- Drop the "investment is paying off" claim, or heavily qualify it.

## The overall rise is partly a mix effect

Repairs is the lowest-scoring division, and its share of respondents fell from about 37% to about 24%. Fewer low scorers in the pool pushes the overall average up even if nobody's views changed. These figures are my estimates, using 2025 response rates applied to 2026 headcounts, so treat them as approximate:

- **Respondent-weighted index (as reported):** 65 → 68
- **2026 scores at 2025 respondent weights:** about 67.2, so roughly 0.8 of the 3-point rise is mix
- **Headcount-weighted (each division weighted by staff numbers):** about 64.2 → 66.9

There is still a genuine improvement of around 2.5 points. But the headline 68 overstates the level, and "highest since 2019" needs checking against a headcount-weighted series. The report also shows no pre-2025 data, so that claim currently can't be verified.

**Suggested fix:** Report a headcount-weighted index alongside the raw one, and show the historical series.

## Causal claims go further than the evidence

**3. The theme data don't link to Repairs.** Table 2 is organisation-wide. The +8 on tools could come from any division, and Repairs now makes up less than a quarter of respondents. If the tools gain is concentrated in Repairs, show that with theme scores by division. If it isn't, the "consistent with the investment" argument weakens.

**4. Recommendation 5.1 picks one component without evidence.** The 2025 programme had three parts: vans and tablets, a revised bonus scheme, and director-led briefings. The report recommends extending only the briefings, "given the improvement it has delivered". Nothing in the data isolates the briefings' effect. Arguably the tools score points more to the equipment. The recommendation may still be reasonable, but it should be framed as a judgement, not a finding.

**5. Before-and-after is not proof the programme worked.** Without a comparison group, other explanations remain open, such as wider labour-market conditions or changes in management. The conclusion "can be confident that the 2025 engagement programme worked" should be softened to something like "results are encouraging and consistent with the programme having an effect".

## Workload analysis

**6. The vacancy explanation is plausible, but "specific, measurable cause" overstates it.**
- Housing Management now supplies about 41% of respondents, more than its 31% share of headcount. You would expect its concerns to dominate free text regardless.
- Housing Management engagement actually rose (69 → 70), which sits awkwardly with it being the source of the organisation's main problem.
- Show workload theme scores by division, and the count or share of workload comments by division relative to respondents. Also clarify whether the 610 headcount includes the 41 vacant posts.

## Smaller points

- **"Like for like":** the instrument is unchanged, which is true and good. The *sample* is not like for like. The report and your summary should distinguish the two.
- **Statistical noise:** changes of ±1–2 points (Housing Management, Central Services, "priorities", "workload") are probably within the margin of error. Ask the provider for confidence intervals, or flag which changes are statistically significant.
- **Recommendation 5.3:** repeating "the same method" should include a specific fix for reaching Repairs. Otherwise 2027 inherits the same problem.
- **Recommendation 5.2:** halving vacancies is a good, measurable target. Consider adding a linked measure, such as workload agreement in Housing Management in 2027.

## Suggested revised conclusion

> "Engagement improved modestly in 2026, by around 2–3 points once changes in who responded are accounted for, and three of four divisions improved. Repairs and Maintenance showed the largest reported gain, but its response rate halved to 31%, so this result should be treated with caution until we understand why. Tools and equipment scores rose most, and workload remains the main concern, with Housing Management vacancies a likely contributor. We recommend extending elements of the Repairs programme on a trial basis, prioritising Housing Management recruitment, and fixing survey access for operatives before March 2027."

This version is still positive. It is also defensible if an Executive Team member reads Table 1 closely, and the current version isn't.
